title: Face to face (2 and 3 John)
hookLine: two postcards from the elder: I'd rather not write with ink, but talk face to face
carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder

lines: I'D RATHER NOT WRITE IT IN INK.
cards: Count the times this week you texted someone you could have called, or called someone you could have visited. No judgment; it's how a lot of life works now.
Long ago, a church leader who calls himself simply the elder felt the pull the other way. Two of his notes survive in the Bible, Second and Third John, each only a page or so long.
Both end with almost the same line: I have more to say, but I'd rather not say it in ink. I'd rather come and talk to you face to face.

teach.h: THE ELECT LADY: A WOMAN, OR A CHURCH?
teach.b: Second John is addressed "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth." Nobody knows who she is. She might be a woman who hosted a church in her home.
Some readers think the elect lady names a whole congregation, with her children as its members.
The note repeats the heart of First John: love one another, walk in his commandments, and beware teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh.
Third John is a personal note to "the wellbeloved Gaius." There's praise for Gaius, who opened his home to traveling teachers.

There's a complaint about a man named Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence among them," and who turned those travelers away. And a good word for someone called Demetrius. Then both notes end the same way.

In the King James Bible, Second John says: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full."

teach.h: THE GREEK SAYS MOUTH TO MOUTH.
teach.b: The Greek is more bodily than the English: not face to face but mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma.

teach.h: A WEEK OF LOVE, ENDING IN PERSON.
teach.b: The elder knew what ink can't carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder, the look on someone's face when they finally understand.

teach.h: THAT OUR JOY MAY BE FULL.
teach.b: That closes a week about love, from greater than your heart to face to face, ending with an elder who'd rather show up in person.

how: In Christian communities, hospitality and visiting, especially of the sick, the homebound and travelers, are a traditional part of life together, and 3 John's praise of Gaius is sometimes read as a picture of that welcome.

games.q: you're the elder. you have many things to say to people you love. what do you do?
o: write a long letter covering everything.
send a short note and promise to come in person.
wait for them to write first.
games.why: "I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full."

practice: Bring to mind someone you mostly know through a screen these days, a grandparent, an old friend, a neighbor you only wave at, and picture their actual face, the way it moves when they laugh.

In the quiet, choose one small way to be in the same room soon, a coffee, a walk, a knock on the door, or a call where they can hear your voice if a visit isn't possible. If you pray, hold their name for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Stoma. Greek for mouth: the elder's own word for face to face, mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma, the joy that ink can't carry and a visit can.

orig.note: Greek: mouth to mouth, the elder's phrase in 2 John 12 and 3 John 14, usually translated face to face.
